title: On the relaxation problem in statistical mechanics
abstract: We reformulate the relaxation problem in statistical mechanics by making explicit what are the \emph{operational} objects subject to relaxation: the local time statistics of the recorded signal $Z(t)$. These local time statistics are simply the estimated histograms of observations $\{Z(t_i)\}_{i=1}^M$ performed at uniformly random times $\{t_i\}_{i=1}^M$ by a clockless observer. The subject of prediction is a belief about a future fresh out-of-sample reading of a measurement outcome whose distribution is inferred from the mathematical model believed to be true. For finite bounded systems of $N\ge 1$ degrees of freedom global irreversible relaxation of predictions can occur but special initial conditions exist. The form of the predictions depends on certain loss functions whose choice is up to the particular observer. Finally, entropy is given a learning interpretation as mutual information between the observer and the unknown past of the system under consideration and, in complete generality, its stationary value depends on the information available.
summary: This work reinterprets the relaxation problem in statistical mechanics by focusing on what an observer can actually measure: local time statistics. It shows that the best prediction of future states is determined by minimizing the generalization error, linking fundamental physics concepts like entropy to information theory. This offers a dynamical justification for inference in non-equilibrium systems.
main_problem: The paper reformulates the relaxation problem in statistical mechanics by shifting focus from fundamental dynamics to the operational statistics derived from measurements.
main_result: The optimal prediction for future states, based on observed local time statistics, is governed by minimizing the generalization error, which is shown to be related to the system's entropy.
method: The authors use an information-theoretic approach, interpreting entropy as mutual information and employing concepts from machine learning generalization error to derive dynamical predictions.
model_or_system: The system consists of a bounded set of $N$ degrees of freedom evolving deterministically, $Z(t)$, which is observed by a 'clockless observer' collecting samples at random times.
key_observables: Local time statistics (estimated histograms), generalization error ($L^*_T$), and entropy (interpreted as mutual information).
important_parameters: The number of degrees of freedom ($N$), the time window ($T$), and the measurement resolution ($\Delta	heta, \Delta\omega$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the system follows deterministic dynamics and that the observer samples measurements uniformly at random times.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the Alice/Bob setup for prediction uncertainty and show the decay of the generalization error and global entropy as a function of measurement time or resolution.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the operational framework using local time statistics, then deriving the prediction rule via generalization error minimization, and finally analyzing the convergence of entropy and mutual information in the thermodynamic limit.
why_interesting: It provides a novel, information-theoretic lens to view irreversible processes, connecting concepts from statistical mechanics directly to modern machine learning inference principles.
